opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at first it just didn't seem like something that could happen. Yann is someone I've looked up to for my whole career. He's a Turing Award winner, one of the people who basically invented the field I work in, and for years he's had this very established role leading research at a huge company. So when the idea of starting something new came up, my first instinct was, why would someone at that stage, with that stature, want to go through the chaos of a startup? Fundraising, hiring, building infrastructure from scratch. It's a very different life from running a big research lab.

There was also a psychological barrier on my side. We've collaborated, and I know him well enough to talk ideas with him very directly, but there's still a big difference between "a senior figure I respect and write papers with" and "a co-founder I'm building a company with day to day." It felt almost presumptuous to imagine it.

What changed my mind was realizing how strongly he believes in his direction. He's been saying for years that large language models alone won't get us to real intelligence, that we need systems that understand the physical world, build world models, and can plan and reason. That's very close to what I care about too, especially from the vision side. At some point it became clear that, for him, this wasn't about prestige or comfort. He wanted to prove the idea, and he felt the best way to do that now was to build something focused and independent rather than keep arguing for it from inside a big organization.

Once I saw it that way, it stopped feeling unimaginable. It felt like a natural next step for both of us, because we were pointing at the same problem and both thought it deserved a serious, dedicated effort.

r001.rationale: The response describes LeCun as an established research leader and a senior figure Xie respected and wrote papers with, which made imagining him as a startup co-founder seem presumptuous.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, in my mind Yann was always a scientist. He's been at Meta for over a decade, running FAIR, and before that he was a professor at NYU for a long time. When I think of Yann, I think of someone who writes papers, gives talks, argues with people on Twitter about whether LLMs are a dead end. That's his natural habitat. He's a researcher through and through, and he's the kind of person who really cares about getting the science right rather than getting a product out the door.

So when the idea came up of him stepping away from Meta and actually founding a company, my first reaction was, this doesn't fit the picture I have of him. Starting a company means fundraising, hiring, dealing with investors, thinking about go-to-market. Those are things I never associated with Yann. He's 65, he's a Turing Award winner, he has basically nothing left to prove. Why would he want to put himself through the grind of a startup?

The other thing is that Yann's research agenda, the whole world model and JEPA direction, is deliberately long-horizon. It's not the kind of thing where you can show a demo in six months and raise your next round. It goes against the current mainstream, which is scaling autoregressive LLMs. So from a business standpoint, I couldn't easily see how you package that into a company that investors would understand, at least not in the usual way.

What changed my mind, I think, is realizing that for Yann it's less about being an entrepreneur and more about having the freedom to pursue that agenda without the constraints of a big company whose priorities have shifted toward LLM products. In that sense, the company is a vehicle for the research, not the other way around. Once I saw it that way, it made a lot more sense to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes Yann as a scientist and researcher “through and through,” then says founding a company did not fit Xie’s picture of him.
